1.text:
"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm" is three letters of the Arabic alphabet and nothing else, and the first fact about the line is that it has no verb, no subject and no object, so a reader is given letters where a sentence was expected. The word used for these letters means things cut short from their length, and they come at the beginning of twenty-nine chapters of the Qur'ān, sometimes as the name of a chapter itself, as in Ta Ha, Ya Sin, Sad and Qaf. Two ways of reading them have come down. One takes them as names of the sūrah, or as symbols of the divine names, and the other leaves them where the shortest reading in the sources leaves them, with the meaning known to God alone, and that is why no commentary and no explanation of them has been carried back from the earliest generation: the Companions and those after them did not settle what the letters were for, and a later reader is not able to do what they left undone. What the chapter is doing by opening this way can be seen without knowing their meaning, and this is the part the sources press on. The book that follows is made of words, and words are made of these letters; they are used in ordinary speech, and one person can say to another, my son recites Alif, Ba, Ta, and yet no one can produce a chapter like what is built out of them. So the letters stand at the front as a sign of the challenge, a purpose without a meaning, and the wisdom in the Qur'ān reaches even the pieces it is made of. The sūrah that begins this way is about to describe a book which has no doubt in it, and the distance between those three letters and that claim is the whole sermon: speech a person can repeat, and a book no one can answer.

**The letters that begin certain sūrahs.**

Alif Lām Mīm – letters like these begin certain sūrahs of the Qur’ān. Although they have no meaning in themselves, they do however have a purpose. Muqatta‘at, which in Arabic means abbreviated or shortened letters, are symbolic letter combinations. They appear respectively at the beginning 29 chapters of the Quran in the form of Alif Lam Mim, Ha Mim, Nun, Ayn Sin, Qaf, etc. They also appear as chapter names, such as Ta Ha, Ya Sin, Sad and Qaf.

**No commentary has been transmitted.**

The Surah begins with the Arabic letters Alif, Lam and Mim (equivalents of A, L and M). Several Surahs begin with a similar combination of letters, for example, Ha, Mim, or Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. But the majority of the blessed Companions and the generation next to them, the Tabi’ in, and also the later authoritative scholars have preferred the view that the isolated letters are symbols or mysteries, the meaning of which is known to Allah alone or may have been entrusted as a special secret to the Holy Prophet not to be communicated to anyone else. That is why no commentary or explanation of these letters has at all been reported from him.

**Names of the sūrah, or symbols of the Divine Names.**

According to certain commentators, the isolated letters are the names of the Surahs at the beginning of which they occur. According to others, they are the symbols of the Divine Names. Alif lām mīm God knows best what He means by these letters.

**A purpose without a meaning.**

Since there is divine wisdom contained in everything in the Qur’ān, these letters point to the miracle of the Qur’ān, made up of the letters which make up the words we speak. Therefore, when sūrahs begin with letters in this way, they are usually followed with a verse about the Qur’ān, as we see in this sūrah. This is because the words that are used in speech are usually comprised of one, two, three, four, or five letters." It is also said that only Allah knows the meaning of these disjointed letters; while some maintain that it is an oath that He made. It is also said Alif stands for Allah's blessings (ala'uh), Lam for His kindness (lutfuh) and Mim for His dominion (mulkuh). It is also said that Alif stands for the beginning of the Name Allah, Lam for the beginning of His Name the Kind (al-Latif) and Mim for the beginning of His Name the Glorious (al-Majid). Two longer readings follow, one of them from the earliest generation, and both leave the letters where the verse leaves them.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Each of these letters is pronounced separately without the addition of a vowel sound after it. So, the technical term for them is (Mugatta at: isolated letters). The great commentator Al-Qurtubi has adopted this view of the matter, which is summarized below: "According to Amir Al-Sha'bi, Sufyan Al-Thawri and many masters of the science of Hadith, every revealed book contains certain secret signs and symbols and mysteries of Allah; the isolated letters too are the secrets of Allah in the Holy Qur'an, and hence they are among the (Mutashabihat: of hidden meaning), the meaning of which is known to Allah alone, and it is not permissible for us even to enter into any discussion with regard to them. The isolated letters are not, however, without some benefit to us. Firstly, to believe in them and to recite them is in itself a great merit. Secondly, in reciting them we receive spiritual blessings from the unseen world, even if we are not aware of the fact. "The Blessed Caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali and most of the Companions like Abdullah ibn Mas'ud firmly held the view that these letters are the secrets of Allah, that we should believe in them as having descended from Allah and recite them exactly in the form in which they have descended, but should not be inquisitive about their meanings, which would be improper".

2.text:
"This is the Book" is the first sentence of a long passage about what a person does with a book, and the word used to point at it, that, is the one used for a thing at a distance, which the sources take as a sign of its rank and not of its place: what is being named is high, and the reader is being brought near to it rather than told where it is. "There is no doubt about it" then closes the only door a hearer would otherwise knock on. The word for doubt covers suspicion as well as denial, and the phrase is read in two ways, either as a statement about the book, that nothing in it is open to question, or as a prohibition, that no doubt is to be raised against it; both readings come to the same place, and the second is the harder one, because a thousand objections from small minds do not touch a book that is not changed by them. "a guide for those mindful of Allah" is the half that sounds like a limit, and it is the part the sources argue most about, since a book with no doubt in it ought to guide everyone. The answer given is that the mind, the word from which the God-fearing take their name, is a protecting of oneself, and a guidance is received by the one who is open to it: the limitation is in the vessel and not in the book, in the eye and not in the light. Then the two halves are one argument, and the whole is a claim about what this book is and what it does. It is the same claim the chapter opened with in a different register, since three letters were thrown down first, and now the book they belong to is described; the next verses will show the three who receive it and the two who do not, and the division has begun here rather than at the reproach.

**A word that points at something distant.**

The sentence "That Book has no doubt in it" raises a grammatical and exegetical problem, for the first phrase in the Arabic text reads as :Dhcilikal kitab. Now, the word dhalika (that) is used to point out a distant thing, while the word kitab (book) obviously refers to the Holy Qur'an itself, which is present before us. That meaning this Book which Muhammad recites in it there is no doubt no uncertainty that it is from God the negation lĀ rayba fĪhi is the predicate of dhĀlika; the use of the demonstrative here is intended to glorify the Book.

**Doubt, and the God-fearing.**

The Book, is the Qur'an, and Rayb means doubt. (In which there is no Rayb), means about which there is no doubt. " The meaning of this is that the Book, the Qur'an, is without a doubt revealed from Allah. The Arabic word for the God-fearing is Muttaqin, derived from Taqwa which literally means "to fear, to refrain from", and in Islamic terminology it signifies fearing Allah and refraining from the transgression of His commandments. " Ibn 'Abbas also said that Al-Muttaqin means, "Those who fear Allah's punishment, which would result if they abandoned the true guidance that they recognize and know.

**An objection, and an answer.**

There are two ways in which doubt or suspicion may arise with regard to the validity or authenticity of statement. So, in spite of the doubts and objections of a thousand men of small or perverse understanding, it would still be true to say that there is no doubt in this book - either with regard to it having been revealed by Allah, or with regard to its contents. This explanation should be sufficient to remove the objection that guidance is needed much more by those who are not God-fearing, for now we know that the specification of the God-fearing does not entail a denial of guidance to those who not possess this qualification. But it guides only those who are sincere in their search for truth, and who are anxious to be guided.

**Which book, and for whom.**

(This is the Scripture), i.e. this is the Book that Muhammad ﷺ is reciting to you; (whereof there is no doubt). It is also said that (This is the Scripture) refers to the Guarded Tablet. It is also said (this is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt) means there is no doubt that the description and traits of Muhammad are found in the Torah and Gospel. This is the Qur’ān, in which there is nothing of any doubt, neither in terms of its origin, nor in terms of its meaning. It is the word of Allah, guiding those who are mindful of Allah to the way that leads to Him. This is the writing in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the godwary. And the spiritual reading takes the two halves together, so that the writing, the tablet and the heart are named in one breath.

3.text:
"who believe in the unseen, establish prayer" and then "and donate from what We have provided for them" — three acts in one line, and they are the content of the mindfulness the previous verse had named, so that a description of a state of heart becomes a description of what a person does. The first act is about what cannot be reached by the senses, and the sources press the difference between knowing a thing in the mind and believing it: that kind of knowledge is possessed even by Satan, and it leaves him where he was, so belief in what is hidden is a thing a person commits themselves to rather than a conclusion they arrive at. The second act is prayer, and the verb used for it is not the one for performing a thing once but the one for setting a thing up and keeping it in place, upright and complete, which is why the same line is read as a command to establish it rather than to say it. The third is spending, and the phrasing is careful in a way that has been argued over for the whole of this chapter: it comes out of what has been provided, and no amount is fixed by the words themselves, which is how one reading takes it as the required poor-due and another as spending at large. The provision is named as His giving, so that the one who gives is not the owner of the thing given, and the mercy of it is that a person is asked to spend out of what they have been handed rather than to produce something of their own. These three stand in order, belief, prayer, and then what is done with what was provided, and the verse after this carries the rest of the account, which is where the earlier revelation and the Hereafter arrive.

**Faith in the unseen.**

who believe in that is who accept the truth of the Unseen what is hidden from them of the Resurrection Paradise and the Fire; and maintain the prayer that is to say who perform it giving it its proper due; and of what We have provided them that is of what we have bestowed upon them expend in obedience to God;. (Who believe in the unseen), that which is hidden from them such as Paradise, hell, the Bridge over hell, the Scale, the Resurrection, the Reckoning, etc. It is also said that this means: that they believe in the unseen which is revealed in the Qur'an and also in that which is not revealed therein. They believe in the revelation that Allah sent down to you, O Prophet, and in that which He revealed to all the other prophets before you (peace be upon them), without distinction; and they have a definite belief in the Afterlife, with its rewards and punishments. When this leads to a discovery, it is transformed into faith in the unseen.

**A comprehensive definition of belief.**

The Holy Qur'an has provided a comprehensive definition of 'Iman in only two words " "Believe in the unseen". For, a mental knowledge of the truth is possessed by Satan himself, and even by many disbelievers - for example, they knew very well that the Holy Prophet was truthful and that his teachings were true, but they did not have faith in him nor did they accept his teachings with their heart, and hence they are not Muslims.

**The verb used for prayer.**

" The verb employed by the Holy Qur'an here is Yuqimuna (generally rendered in English translations as "they establish", which comes from the word Iqamaha signifying "to straighten out"). (And establish worship), they perform to completion the five prescribed prayers, including the ablution that precedes them, the bowing and prostrations which are parts of them and also what is obligated in these prayers in terms of appointed timing.

**Spending out of what is provided.**

"Spend out of what We have provided them" inspires us to spend in the way of Allah by drawing our attention to the fact that anything and everything we possess is a gift from Allah and His trust in our hands, and that even if we spend all our possessions in the way of Allah, it would be proper and just and no favour to Him. But Allah in His mercy asks us to spend in His way "out of' what he has provided - that is, only a part and not the whole. (And spend of that We have bestowed upon them), and of that which We have given them of wealth they give to charity. It is also said that this means: they give the poor-due (Zakat) from their wealth.

**Zakah, or spending in general.**

(And spend out of what We have provided for them) means, "The Zakah due on their wealth. (And spend out of what We have provided for them) means, "A man's spending on his family. " Juwaybir narrated from Ad-Dahhak, "General spending (in charity) was a means of drawing nearer to Allah, according to one's discretion and capability. The benefits of the commandments are the reason for them, and the last of the three acts is the one the sources argue about most.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The next two verses delineate the characteristic qualities of the God-fearing, suggesting that these are the people who have received guidance, whose path is the straight path, and that he who seeks the straight path should join their company, adopt their beliefs and their way of life. It is perhaps in order to enforce this suggestion that the Holy Qur'an, immediately after pointing out the attributes peculiar to the God-fearing, proceeds to say: It is these who are on guidance given by their Lord, and it is just these who are successful. The delineation of the qualities of the God-fearing in these two verses also contains, in essence, a definition of Faith ('Iman) and an account of its basic tenets and of the fundamental principles of righteous conduct: Who believe in the unseen, and are steadfast in Salah and spend out of what We have provided them. Thus, the first of the two verses, mentions three qualities of the God-fearing - belief in the unseen, being steadfast in Salah, and spending in the way of Allah.

4.text:
"and who believe in what has been revealed to you O Prophet and what was revealed before you" widens belief in two directions at once, and the second half of that is the difficulty the sources sit with, since what came before had been changed by the people who were given it. The requirement stands anyway, and the reason is in the wording: the verse does not separate what was revealed from what was revealed before, and a Muslim is asked to affirm a book they do not hold in their hands, because this book confirms what is true in the others and stands over them. The companions of the Prophet are read as the first hearers of this, and the same line is turned against those who were given the Book before them, since believing in the earlier revelation is the thing they are asked for in the verses that follow, and a faith that stops at one book cannot be the faith described here. Then the last phrase, "and have sure faith in the Hereafter", is what the whole list has been building toward, and the word used is a certainty that leaves no room in the heart for doubt, so belief in what was revealed and belief in what comes after death are placed on one level. The sources ask what a person is required to say about books they cannot check, and the answer given is that the same book which commands the belief also testifies to what remains in them; and the Hereafter named here is the reason the acts of the previous verse are done at all, since a prayer and a spending are weighed on that day. Four qualities have now been listed, and the next verse closes the account with what they are worth.

**The earlier Divine Books.**

Commenting on this verse, the blessed Companions Abdullah ibn Masud and Abdullah ibn Abbs have said that in the days of the Holy Prophet God-fearing Muslims were of two kinds, - those who used to be associators and disbelievers but accepted Islam, and those who used to be among the people of the Book (that is, Jews and Christians) but embraced Islam later on; the preceding verse refers to the first group, and this verse to the second. Hence this verse specifically mentions belief in the earlier Divine Books along with belief in the Holy Qur'an, for, according to the Hadith, people in the second group deserve a double recompense, firstly, for believing in and following the earlier Books before the Holy Qur'an came to replace them, and secondly, for believing in and following the Holy Qur'an when it came as the final Book of Allah. Even today it is obligatory for every Muslim to believe in the earlier Divine Books except that now the belief has to take this form: everything that Allah has revealed in the earlier Books is true (excepting the changes and distortions introduced by selfish people), and that it was incumbent upon the people for whom those Books had been sent to act according to them, but now that all the earlier Books and Shari'ahs have been abrogated, one must act according to the Holy Qur'an alone.3. and who believe in what has been revealed to you namely the Qur’ān; and what was revealed before you that is the Torah the Gospel and other scriptures; and of the Hereafter they are certain that is they know it is real.

**What was revealed before you.**

(And who have faith in what is revealed to you and in what was revealed before you.) means, "They believe in what Allah sent you with, and in what the previous Messengers were sent with, they do not distinguish between (believing) them, nor do they reject what they brought from their Lord." (And who believe in that which is revealed unto thee (Muhammad) of the Qur'an (and that which was revealed before you) of scriptures given to all the prophets, (and are certain of the Hereafter), they believe in resurrection after death and in the bliss of Paradise, referring here specifically to 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his followers. They believe in the revelation that Allah sent down to you, O Prophet, and in that which He revealed to all the other prophets before you (peace be upon them), without distinction; and they have a definite belief in the Afterlife, with its rewards and punishments.

**Belief in a book one does not possess.**

Before we proceed, we may point out that in speaking of faith in the hereafter as one of the qualities of the God-fearing, the Holy Qur'an does not use the word yu'minuna (believe) but the word yuqinuna (have complete certitude), for the opposite of belief is denial, and that of certitude is doubt and hesitation. This verse is also the attribute of the godwary and the affirmation of their faith in the Qur'an as well as in all the messages and marks that came down from heaven on the tongue of the prophets. And those who have faith in what has been sent down to thee and what was sent down before thee and who are certain of the next world.

**A warning to those who were given the Book.**

(O you who have been given the Book (Jews and Christians)! Believe in what We have revealed (to Muhammad) confirming what is (already) with you)(4:47), and,. (Say (O Muhammad): "O People of the Book (Jews and Christians)! You have nothing until you act according to the Tawrah (Torah), the Injil (Gospel), and what has been revealed to you from your Lord (the Qur'an).")(5:68). However, the faith that many Arabs have in the religion of Islam as it was revealed to Muhammad might be more complete, encompassing and firmer than the faith of the People of the Book who embraced Islam.

**Certainty in the Hereafter.**

Those had longer days of practice, but this community has more reward for obedience. The Lord of the Worlds praises them and approves of them because of that, and He accepts their faith. A man who amasses wealth by usurping what rightfully belongs to others, or who gains petty material ends by adopting unlawful means forbidden by Allah, may declare his faith in the hereafter a thousand times and the Shari'ah may accept him as a Muslim in the context of worldly concerns, but he does not possess the certitude which the Holy Qur'an demands of him. Those who came before had longer days of practice, and the last clause is what the whole verse has been building toward.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This verse speaks of some other attributes of the God-fearing, giving certain details about faith in the unseen with a special mention of faith in hereafter. Exactly as predicted by a Hadith, today we see all around us a proliferation of "knowledge" and of "writing". One of the dangerous forms the process has taken is the indiscriminate translation at least into European languages and the popularization of the sacred books of all possible religious and metaphysical traditions - not only the Hindu, the Chinese or the Japanese, but also the Shamanic or the Red Indian.

5.text:
"It is they who are truly guided by their Lord" closes the list of four qualities with a verdict rather than a command, and the same words return again in "and it is they who will be successful", so the verse is built out of a repetition and nothing else. The praise is for the whole of what was described and not for one part of it taken alone, and the sources ask what a person is given by these two clauses, since guidance and success look like one thing named twice. The answer is that they are two: guidance is the road and success is what is reached at the end of it, and the second is not earned by the first but given with it. Then the direction of both is settled, in this life and in the Hereafter, since what they are given is reward and eternal life in Paradise and safety from the evil they tried to avoid, and the saving is counted as a part of the success rather than as its price. The two readings of the first clause stand side by side in the sources, one taking guidance as the state of being on the road and the other as the light that shows it, and the spiritual reading keeps both, since the lamp is lit in the heart so that what is hidden and what is seen become one thing to the one who believes. After this the chapter turns, and the next verses describe those who were given the same chance and closed themselves, which is why the two groups have to be read against each other: what has been described of the first is the standard the second will be shown against.

**Who the praise is for.**

Those as described in the way mentioned are upon guidance from their Lord those are the ones that will prosper that is who will succeed in entering Paradise and be saved from the Fire. (They are) refers to those who believe in the Unseen, establish the prayer, spend from what Allah has granted them, believe in what Allah has revealed to the Messenger and the Messengers before him, believe in the Hereafter with certainty, and prepare the necessary requirements for the Hereafter by performing good deeds and avoiding the prohibitions. (These) who have these traits, (are on guidance from their Lord), they enjoy favour, mercy and clear exposition that has come down from their Lord, (and these are the successful ones), the ones who shall escape Allah's wrath and torment. It is also said that this refers to those who have apprehended and found what they were seeking and have escaped the evil of that from which they were fleeing, and these are the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ.

**Guidance and success, twice over.**

(And they are the successful) meaning, in this world and the Hereafter. They shall have what they seek and be saved from the evil that they tried to avoid. Therefore, they will have rewards, eternal life in Paradise, and safety from the torment that Allah has prepared for His enemies. The people who possess these qualities are on the path of guidance, and will be successful in this world and the next, gaining what they desire and being saved from what they fear. Heaven will be their final destination in the life to come.

**The lamp lit in the heart.**

He has lit up the lamp of guidance in their hearts so that what is unseen for others is apparent to them. He has opened up the door of perspicacity for them and put into effect the gaze of solicitude inside their hearts. It is an essential quality of the God-fearing that they always have present before their eyes the whole picture of how people will have to present themselves for judgment before Allah in the hereafter, how their deeds will be assessed and how they will receive reward or punishment according to what they have been doing in this world. These are the men of proximity and presence, and the chapter has now finished telling us who they are.

6.text:
The chapter has finished with the people who are mindful and turns now to their opposite, and the turn is flat rather than dramatic: "As for those who persist in disbelief", and then "it is the same whether you warn them or not", and then "they will never believe". The three parts are one statement, and the middle of them is the strange one, since a warning is given to move a person and here the giving of it changes nothing. The word for disbelief is used in the sense this book gives it, a denial of anything that has been brought, and the sources take the fault to be a settled refusal rather than a shortage of evidence, because the people described here met the message with open hostility while keeping denial inside themselves. That is why the verse is read as being about particular men and about anyone who is like them: some of the sources name men of Makkah and of the Jews, and others leave the line open to whoever closes themselves this way. Then the difficulty the whole passage raises is faced at length in the sources, since a refusal that was written down beforehand looks like one that was put there, and the answer given is that the writing follows the refusal rather than causing it, so that the blame rests where the doing rests. The spiritual reading moves the same verse into a different register and asks what is being described at all: it is read as severity and justice turned toward a stranger who was far off, with the point that justice and bounty are not the same thing, and what the one does the other does not. The warning is then left standing in the reader's hands, since whoever recites this chapter is doing the very thing this verse has just called useless to some, and the next two verses describe what has been done to them instead.

**The terminology of disbelief.**

In the terminology of the Shari ah, kufr signifies the denial of any of those things in which it is obligatory to believe. As we have said, the first two verses of this Surah speak of those disbelievers who had become so stubborn and obstinate in their denial and disbelief that they were not prepared to hear the truth or to consider a clear argument. (As for the disbelievers) who remain firm in their disbelief, (whether thou warn them), instil fear into them by means of the Qur'an, (or thou warm them not) or you do not instil fear into them, (it is all one for them; they believe not), they do not want to believe. It is also said that they will not believe as it is in Allah's knowledge.

**Open hostility, and secret denial.**

On the one hand were those who came out in open hostility and rejection, and whom the Holy Qur'an has termed as kafirun (disbelievers); on the other hand were those who did not, on account of their moral depravity and greed, had even the courage to speak out their minds and to express their disbelief clearly, but adopted the way of deceit and duplicity. But they nursed denial and rejection in their hearts, and would, in the company of disbelievers, assure them that they had nothing to do with Islam, but mixed with Muslims in order to deceive them and to spy on them. People of the first kind are those whose path is the object of the prayer at the end of the Surah Al-Fatihah, ‌ : the path of those on whom You have bestowed Your grace", and people of the second kind are those against whose path refuge has been sought. Those who reject what Allah revealed to His Messenger continue on the wrong path in their stubbornness.

**Whether the warning makes any difference.**

As for the disbelievers the likes of Abū Jahl Abū Lahab and such; alike it is for them whether you have warned them or have not warned them they do not believe as God knows very well so do not hope that they will believe read a-andhartahum pronouncing both hamzas or by not pronouncing the second making it an alif instead and inserting an alif between the one not pronounced and the other one or leaving this insertion; al-indhār ‘warning’ is to give knowledge of something and simultaneously instil an element of fear. Since Allah has written that they would do so, it does not matter if you (O Muhammad) warn them or not, they would still have disbelieved in what you were sent with. Allah informed him that none would believe except for those whom He decreed happiness for in the first place, and none would stray except those who Allah has decreed to do so in the first place. Much as people are urged by him to submit to the will of God, they baulk at doing so, because it would mean demolishing the world they have made for themselves. It is difficult also for him to convey his message to highly placed individuals who are afraid that, if they follow an ‘insignificant’ person, they will thereby suffer some diminution of their own personal glory.

**Why people close themselves this way.**

If one hears it with an open mind, one will know in one’s heart that it is nothing else but truth. However, where society is rigidly bound by age-old conventions, people are less concerned with opening their minds to divine realities than they are with supporting the vested interests of the existing system. The minds of those who do not consider the call of truth seriously, who are proud and worldly in their attitude, are covered with an invisible veil which makes them impervious to the truth. Justice and bounty are then distinguished, which is how the chapter keeps the verse from becoming a sentence about God's caprice.

**What else the same passage holds.**

After affirming the Holy Qur'an as the Book of Guidance and as being beyond all doubt, the first five verses of the present Surah refer to those who derive full benefit from this Book and whom the Holy Qur'an has named as Mu'minun (true Muslims) or Muttaqun (the God-fearing), and also delineate their characteristic qualities which distinguish them from others.

7.text:
"Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing" is a picture of a thing closed from the outside, and the second half, "and their sight is covered", finishes the set of three, so that the inside of a person, the ear and the eye are each dealt with in turn. The word for the seal is a stamp put on a thing so that what is inside stays inside, and the sources ask at once which came first, the sealing or the refusal, because another verse puts it that what they did had rusted their hearts. The two have to be read together, and the reading given is that God is the creator of what they do and the stain remains theirs, so the seal is a judgement upon a heart already turned rather than a lock set on a willing one. Then the last clause, "They will suffer a tremendous punishment", is the reason the verse does not stop at the seal: what is described in this life is the state, and what is named at the end of it is what the state becomes. The spiritual reading keeps the same word and divides the people into two cases, one sealed with estrangement and one with perplexity, a traveller who has lost the road and a man who is kept back from it by talk, and this second half of the reading is where the chapter's warning about the seal is hardest to hear, since a person who is told they are sealed is being told what they have made of themselves. The next verse opens with a third group, and they have neither the frankness of the disbeliever nor the safety of the believer.

**A stamp on three things.**

God has set a seal on their hearts impressing on them and making certain that no good enters them; and on their hearing in which He has deposited something so that they cannot profit from the truth they hear; and on their eyes is a covering that is a veil so that they do not see the truth; and for them there will be a mighty chastisement that is intense and everlasting. Allah has set a seal on their hearts and on their hearing, and on their eyes there is a covering. (Allah hath sealed their hearts), stamped their hearts, (and their hearing, and on their eyes there is a covering), on their eyes there is a shield (and theirs will be an awful doom) an awful torment in the Hereafter. Allah has sealed their hearts, locking inside them their falsehood, and has placed a seal on their hearing, so that they do not listen to nor accept the truth. He has put a cover over their eyes, so that they do not see the truth in its clarity.

**The rust and the stain.**

(Nay! But on their hearts is the Ran (stain) which they used to earn)" (83:14). Therefore, Allah sealed their hearts, hearing and sight, and they could neither see the guidance nor hear, comprehend or understand.

**An objection about the sealing.**

So, there is no occasion here to raise the objection that if Allah Himself has sealed their hearts and blocked their senses, they are helpless and cannot be held responsible for being disbelievers, and hence they should not be punished for what they have not themselves chosen to do. If we consider the two verses (2:7 and 83:14) together, we can easily see why they should be punished in adopting the way of arrogance and pride they have, willfully and out of their own choice, destroyed their capacity for accepting the truth, and thus they themselves are the authors of their own ruin. But Allah, being Creator of all the actions of His creatures, has in verse 2:7 attributed to Himself the setting of a seal on the hearts and the ears of the disbelievers, and has thus pointed out that when these people insisted, as a matter of their own choice, on destroying their aptitude for receiving the truth, Allah produced, as is His way in such cases, the state of insensitivity in their hearts and senses. Al-Qurtubi said, "The Ummah has agreed that Allah has described Himself with sealing and closing the hearts of the disbelievers, as a punishment for their disbelief.

**Two seals, two cases.**

The seal of estrangement was placed on someone's heart, and he remained in unbelief. The seal of perplexity was placed on another's heart, and he remained in lassitude. That one was a stranger, driven away, the road lost, and this one was helpless, stuck in the road, kept back from the Friend by other than the Friend. Someone who escapes from unbelief reaches familiarity, but someone who escapes from himself reaches friendship.

**Whom the verse names first.**

This refers in particular to the Jews Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab. It is also said that it refers to the idolaters of Makkah 'Utbah [Ibn Rabi'ah], Shaybah [Ibn Rabi'ah] and al-Walid [Ibn al-Mughirah]. However, where society is rigidly bound by age-old conventions, people are less concerned with opening their minds to divine realities than they are with supporting the vested interests of the existing system. The cover over the eyes is the last of the three, and it is what the warning had already been about.

**What else the same passage holds.**

These two verses tell us that the other world is the place where one would receive the real punishment for one's disbelief or for some of one's sins. One may, however, receive some punishment for certain sins even in this world. Such a punishment sometimes takes a very grievous form - that is, the divine favour which helps one to reform oneself is withdrawn, so that, ignoring how one's deeds are to be assessed on the Day of Judgment, one keeps growing in disobedience and sin, and finally comes to lose even the awareness of evil. In delineating such a situation certain elders have remarked that one punishment for an evil deed is another evil deed which comes after, and one reward for a good deed is another good deed which comes after. According to a Hadith, when a man commits a sin, a black dot appears on his heart; this first dot disturbs him just as a smudge on a white cloth is always displeasing to us; but if, instead of asking Allah's pardon for the first sin, he proceeds to commit a second, another dot shows up, thus, with every new sin the black dots go on multiplying till the whole heart turns dark, and now he can no longer see good as good nor evil as evil, and grows quite incapable of making such distinctions.

8.text:
"And there are some who say" is how this group is introduced, and the introduction is a quotation rather than a description, which is the whole difficulty of the verse: "We believe in Allah and the Last Day", and then "yet they are not true believers". Then the last half of the verse is the judgement, and it is put flatly, since they are not believers, and this is the only place in the chapter where a group is introduced by their own mouth and answered in the same breath. The sources collect what is known of their characteristics at length, when they speak these words and whom they are spoken before, and the answer given there is a thing a reader can hear for themselves: the words are spoken in one company and left off in another, and that is what makes the claim a policy. The moral reading presses further and asks why a person would choose this position at all, and the reason it gives is worldly interest, a safeguarding of themselves in this life and in the next, with the sincere counted as simple and their own course counted as reform. The next verse takes the same people a step on, into what they think they are doing to God.

**A claim with half a belief.**

The following was revealed concerning the hypocrites and some people there are who say ‘We believe in God and the Last Day’ that is in the Day of Resurrection because it is the very last day; but they are not believers the plural import of man in man yaqūl ‘who says’ is taken into account here as expressed by a pronoun hum that expresses this plural meaning. Among the people are those who say, "We have faith in God.

The verse ‌:"We believe in Allah and in the Last Day" shows us how disgusting it is to tell a lie - even the hypocrites, with all their hostility to Islam, tried to refrain from it as far as possible. (Verily, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but it is He Who deceives them), "The hypocrites pronounce, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah' seeking to ensure the sanctity of their blood and money, all the while concealing disbelief."Sa'id said that Qatadah said,.

**Policy, and what it costs them.**

For those who put worldly interests and expediency first, total and unconditional devotion to truth appears unwise, for their true allegiance is to their worldly interests; only on a superficial level can they attach themselves to the truth. They think they are safeguarding themselves in this world, and also qualifying to be considered among the pious. They consider true believers, who act in the interests of truth, to be ruining themselves for no good reason. They call their own policy, on the other hand, one of reform; they prize it because it enables them to pursue a safe course without clashing with anyone; but this just shows how distorted their reasoning is. 9.text:
"They seek to deceive Allah and the believers" names the same people a second time and brings out what they are after, and the answer comes back in one turn: "yet they only deceive themselves", and then "but they fail to perceive it". The difficulty the sources stop on is the first half, since a trick played on believers cannot reach God, and He is named in the sentence anyway; the answer given is that an attempt against His friends is counted as an attempt against Him, and the daring in the phrasing is the point of it, because the same people are described as contravening Him openly while they are being clever in private. Then the harm is traced back to where it began, and the punishment is not something laid on their act from outside but the act's own turn: the harm of the deception and the punishment for it come back to the one who devised it, and no one suffered anything but themselves. The last clause is what makes the verse hard rather than merely neat, since they do not perceive it, and a person who can see no consequence in a thing cannot be warned about it. One line of the sources puts the whole thing as a question about knowledge, since when there is one who knows the true nature of things, the plan of a person who hides is no plan. After this, the verse beneath it names what is in the heart, which is the part they were not able to see, and the increase of it is the answer the chapter gives.

**Why God is named in a trick played on believers.**

Misbehaving Prophets is to misbehave with Allah. These verses denounce the hypocrites for trying to be clever with Allah Himself and to deceive Him, although no one among them could probably have had such an intention or even thought of such a possibility. What they were actually doing was to try to deceive the Holy Prophet and the Muslims. Allah has equated this effort with an attempt to deceive Him, and has thus indicated that a man who is in any way impertinent to a prophet or a man of Allah is ultimately guilty of being impertinent to Allah Himself - this should be true above all in the case of the Holy Prophet who stands in his station at the head of all created beings. They would deceive God and the believers by manifesting the opposite of the unbelief they hide so that they can avoid His rulings in this world; and only themselves they deceive yukhādi‘ūn for the evil consequences of their deception will rebound upon them as they are disgraced in this world when God makes known to His Prophet what they are hiding and they will be punished in the Hereafter; and they are not aware and they do not know that they are actually deceiving themselves mukhāda‘a although a third verbal form from khāda‘a actually denotes a one-way action such as when one says ‘āqabtu al-lissa ‘I punished the thief’ using the third verbal form ‘āqaba; the mention of ‘God’ in this statement is for rhetorical effect; a variant reading for wa-mā yukhādi‘ūna has wa-mā yakhda‘ūna.

**Contravention, and daring.**

(They try to deceive Allah) contravene against Him and denying Him in secret. (Verily, the hypocrites seek to deceive Allah, but it is He Who deceives them), "The hypocrites pronounce, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah' seeking to ensure the sanctity of their blood and money, all the while concealing disbelief."Sa'id said that Qatadah said,.

They would deceive God and the believers; and they only deceive them selves; and they are not aware. The harm of their deception and the punishment for it comes back to themselves so it is as if they have deceived themselves in actuality for they devalue and belittle themselves. No one suffered the harm of their actions but themselves-they cut off their own lifeblood. They think that they can deceive Allah and the believers by acting outside as if they believe, while inside hiding their disbelief; but really, they only deceive themselves, without realising it.

Allah knows all that is secret and hidden, and has told the believers what these people are like. This Ayah means that the hypocrites utter these statements only when they meet you, not because they actually believe what they are saying. They think they are safeguarding themselves in this world, and also qualifying to be considered among the pious. 10.text:
The diagnosis comes last, after two verses of behaviour, and it explains all of it: "There is sickness in their hearts". The word is a disease, and the sources take it first as doubt, then as hypocrisy and the conflict inside a person who is holding two courses at once, so that the sickness is not a weakness of the will but a thing eating at the place where belief sits. The second half is the verse that has been argued over, "and Allah only lets their sickness increase", because an increase sent by God looks like a punishment that has chosen the wrong person, and the reading given is that the growth is not a new thing put into them but the malady left to its own nature, which is how a punishment can be described as forbearance at the same time. Then the verse answers what they thought they had got away with, "They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies", and the pain is tied to the lie rather than to the sickness, since what their tongues put out was contradicted by what was in their hearts. One line of the sources puts the same increase to another use, because that which hardens this people only strengthens the believers, and the difference is in the one who receives it, which is the same answer the second verse of this chapter had given about guidance. The spiritual reading names the sickness by what it is made of, the setting of partners beside Him, and asks what a heart full of that can see; and the parable of the fire and the storm, which is two verses away, is drawn from exactly this state.

**Doubt, hypocrisy, conflict.**

In their hearts is a sickness doubt and hypocrisy which ails their hearts debilitating them; and God has increased their sickness with what He has revealed in the Qur’ān since they disbelieve it; and there awaits them a painful chastisement because they used to lie read yukadhdhibūn to imply that they used to call the Prophet of God a liar or yakdhibūn to imply their mendacity when saying ‘we believe’. (In their hearts is a disease), doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness (so Allah increaseth their disease), increased their doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness. (In their hearts is a disease) means, 'doubt', and,. Because they lied Allah increases the disease of doubts in their hearts, by adding hesitation to their uncertainty, hence they only gain what they deserve.

**A disease hidden in the heart.**

According to the present verse, the disease hidden in their hearts is unbelief and rejection of the truth, which is as much a physical sickness as a spiritual one. In their hearts there is a malady, so Allah has made them grow in their malady. In the terminology of the Holy Qur'an and the Hadith, the word 'disease' is also applied to certain mental or psychic states (we are using the two terms in the original and more comprehensive sense) which hinder man from attaining any degree of spiritual perfection, for they gradually deprive him of the ability to perform good deeds, and even of ordinary human decency, till he meets with his spiritual death.

**The increase, and what it does.**

The third verse indicates why the hypocrites behave so foolishly and why they fail to see the folly of their course: (As for those who believe, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice. But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it will add disgrace to their disgrace.)(9:124-125) and commented, "Evil to their evil and deviation to their deviation. (If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and those who spread false news among the people in Al-Madīnah do not cease, We shall certainly let you overpower them, then they will not be able to stay in it as your neighbors but a little while. Accursed, they shall be seized wherever found, and killed with a (terrible) slaughter)(33:60-61). Allah increases the disease in their hearts, and they reap what they sow.

**What they reap.**

(And a painful doom is theirs), they will have a painful torment in the Hereafter which shall extend to their hearts, (because they lie) in secret, the reference here being to the hypocrites: 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Jadd Ibn Qays and Mu'attib Ibn Qushayr. They will have a painful suffering in the worst parts of Hell because they lied against Allah, and the people, and rejected the message brought by Muhammad ﷺ. The pain of their grievous punishment will reach them in the end.

**The sickness of making partners.**

In the hearts of the hypocrites is the sickness of making partners [with God] shirk and God increases their sickness in their imagining that they have been saved by deceiving the Muslims. In their hearts is a sickness; and God has increased their sickness; and there awaits them a painful chastisement because they used to lie. If the hypocrites had been sincere in their beliefs they would have been safe from the punishment in the hereafter just as they were safe from paying the jizya tax and the like in this world in the manner of polytheists and dhimmīs. For those who put worldly interests and expediency first, total and unconditional devotion to truth appears unwise, for their true allegiance is to their worldly interests; only on a superficial level can they attach themselves to the truth. One further verse is quoted to show that the secret of them is not hidden, and that is where this passage stops.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Now, illness or disease, in the general medical sense, is a state in which a man has lost the balanced proportion of the elements within him necessary to keep him healthy, so that his body can no longer function properly, which may finally lead to his total destruction. The great spiritual master, Junaid of Baghdad, has said that just as the diseases of the body arise from an imbalance among the four humours, the diseases of the heart arise from a surrender to one's physical desires. It is all too obvious that being ungrateful to one's creator and nourisher and going against His commandments is to be spiritually sick. Moreover, to keep this disbelief concealed for the sake of petty worldly gains and not to have the courage to speak out one's mind is no less a disease of the soul. Hypocrisy is a physical disease too in so far as the hypocrite is always shuddering4for fear of being exposed.

11.text:
The pattern of the passage is set by now, and it is put as an event rather than a description: "When they are told", then the thing they are told, "Do not spread corruption in the land, they reply", and then their own words, "We are only peace-makers". What is being asked of them is not to make mischief in the earth, and the word covers disorder in a person's affairs and in the affairs of others, a thing which spoils what was in a good state. The sources take the whole verse to be about a particular people who had come to Madīnah and made their terms with the Prophet, and the same words are then left open to anyone who answers a command the way they did. The difficulty is not in the first half but in the second, since they were not lying about what they wanted; they thought they were putting things right, and this is the part the commentary stops on, because a people who corrupt and call it reform have lost the use of the word. Then the reply is met with an answer of its own in the next verse, and the answer is not an argument but a statement about what they are, which is how the chapter deals with a claim that cannot be settled by debate. The moral reading brings out the reason for the whole position, since such people put worldly interest first, and a policy that keeps them safe in both directions looks to them like peace. A further line is drawn by the sources over the word for land, since corruption in it is not only what a hand does to a field but what a person does to the affairs of others, and the running of the world by new devices is counted in the same balance.

**The warning and the answer.**

When it is said to them that is these latter ‘Do not spread corruption in the land’ through unbelief and hindering people from faith They say ‘We are only putting things right’ that is ‘we are not engaging in corruption’. (And when it is said to them: "Do not make mischief on the earth," they say: "We are only peacemakers.") means, "We seek to make amends between the believers and the People of the Book. (And when it is said unto them), i.e. the Jews (Make not mischief in the land) by preventing people from the Religion of Muhammad ﷺ (they say: we are reformers only), we are reforming it through obedience. When they are told not to ruin things on earth – through their rejection of the truth, their disobedience and so on – they deny doing so, claiming that they only correct things and put them right.

**What corruption in the land means.**

For, among the things which spread disorder in the world, there are some which are commonly recognized to be mischievous and disorderly activities, and hence every sensible and conscientious man refrains from them e.g., theft, robbery, murder, rape etc.; on the other hand, there are some which in their external aspect do not appear to be mischief or disorder, but, working unseen, they have the necessary consequence of destroying the morals of men which, in its turn, opens the door to all kinds of disorder. "Beware, it is, in fact, they who spread disorder, but they are not aware." As these verses report, when the hypocrites were asked not to spread disorder in the land through their prevarication and double dealing, they used to reply emphatically :"We are nothing but reformers. Those who run the world in our day invent ever-new administrative measures to prevent crime, but they not only neglect the very soul of administration, the fear of Allah, but even deploy the means of destroying it - all of which has the necessary consequence that the remedy only helps to feed the malady.

**We are only putting things right.**

When they said We are only putting things right the Real showed them to be liars and He said Truly they are the agents of corruption but they perceive not meaning We are aware of them and have exposed them. They call their own policy, on the other hand, one of reform; they prize it because it enables them to pursue a safe course without clashing with anyone; but this just shows how distorted their reasoning is. If they were to think deeply, they would realize that on earth reform can only come from man giving himself up to God alone, while obstructing any movement aimed at consolidating man’s relationship with the will of his Lord amounts to creating disorder on earth. When they denied the proof of the Real in the thoughts that came to their hearts God took the bless ing away from their states and in its place gave them a deaf ear to the Real.

**They perceive not.**

Verily, they are the ones who make mischief, but they perceive not. Truly they are the agents of corruption but they perceive not. Hence, the deceitful behavior of the hypocrites is an act of mischief, because they deceive the believers by claiming what they do not believe in, and because they give support and loyalty to the disbelievers against the believers. The case of the hypocrites is then read as an act of deception rather than an opinion, which is where the next verse takes hold.

12.text:
One clause turns the previous verse over, "Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors", and then the verse ends on a failure of sight, "but they fail to perceive it". **Beware.**

"Beware, it is, in fact, they who spread disorder, but they are not aware." Truly a-lā ‘truly’ is for alerting intended emphatically they are the agents of corruption but they perceive this not. Truly they are the agents of corruption but they perceive not.

**What they refrained from, and what they did.**

No doubt, they refrained from theft, robbery etc.; it was on this count that they denied their being mischievous, and emphatically asserted that they were serving the cause of order. The truth is that it is they who ruin things, but they do not admit this, nor do they know that their actions are the cause of all ruin. (They are indeed the mischief mongers) by being a hindrance.

**A hindrance, and those who follow it.**

(But they perceive not): the followers do not know that their leaders mislead them. Verily, they are the ones who make mischief, but they perceive not. If they were to think deeply, they would realize that on earth reform can only come from man giving himself up to God alone, while obstructing any movement aimed at consolidating man’s relationship with the will of his Lord amounts to creating disorder on earth. The verse ends on a failure of sight, and the next one returns to the same people in front of a different audience.

13.text:
The answer to the command is now an insult, and the verse keeps both halves of it: "And when they are told", what they are told, "Believe as others believe, they reply", and then the question they answer with, "Will we believe as the fools believe, Indeed". Then the insult is met by a reversal in the same words, "it is they who are fools", and then the last clause, "but they do not know", which is the second time in three verses that a failure of sight has been the end of the verse. The reading is then widened to a lesson about the state of a person who wants the truth to come to them rather than going to it, and their pride and jealousy are what hold them in the position, which is the same disease the earlier verses of this chapter described.

**Believe as the people believe.**

When it is said to them ‘Believe as the people believe’ that is as the Companions of the Prophet s They say ‘Shall we believe as fools believe?’ that is as the ignorant do? ("Believe as the people believe,"), meaning, 'Believe just as the believers believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, Resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire, etc. When they are told to have faith as the companions of Muhammad ﷺ did, they reply, looking down on people and making fun of them, saying “should we have faith like simple-minded people do? (And when it is said unto them) i.e. to Jews, (believe) in Muhammad ﷺ (as the people believe), i.e. 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his companions, (they say: Shall we believe) in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, (as the foolish believe?), i.e. as the stupid and ignorant do, (Surely they are the fools) the stupid and ignorant.

(people) in this verse refers to the blessed Companions of the Holy Prophet because it is just these 'people' who had embraced the Faith and had accepted the Holy Qur'an as the word of Allah while it was being revealed. So, the verse indicates that the only kind of Iman (faith) acceptable to Allah is the one which should be similar to that of the blessed Companions, and that the Iman of others would be worthy of the name only when they believe in the same things in the same way as the Companions did. In other words, the Iman of the Companions is a touchstone for testing the Iman of all the other Muslims; any belief. or deed which departs from their faith and practice, however pleasing in its looks or good in its intention, is not valid according to the Shari ah.

**A touchstone for faith.**

In other words, the Iman of the Companions is a touchstone for testing the Iman of all the other Muslims; any belief. or deed which departs from their faith and practice, however pleasing in its looks or good in its intention, is not valid according to the Shari ah. ("Shall we believe as the fools have believed?") they meant (may Allah curse the hypocrites) the Companions of the Messenger of Allah . And when it is said to them, "Have faith as the people have faith," they say, "Shall we have faith as fools have faith? This is why, according to the majority of the scholars, Allah used the term foolish to include children, when He said,.

The exalted One refutes them saying Truly they are the foolish ones but they know this not. ” In fact, it is they who are the fools, but they are unaware of this. "Those are not the fools, the fools are those who call them fools. The purifiers, the truthful and the Companions of the Messenger are not the fools, and that is the sentence the passage has been building to.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This verse also places before the hypocrites a criterion of true faith (Iman) :"Believe as people have believed". According to the consensus of commentators, the Arabic word Na-s : There is a consensus of commentators on this position. One should also notice that the hypocrites used to call the blessed Companions 'fools' (Sufaha-'). This has always been the way of those who go astray - anyone who tries to show them the right path is, in their eyes, ignorant and stupid. 14.text:
Belief here is a thing spoken in one company and left off in another, and the verse is built on the two meetings. "When they meet the believers they say, We believe" is the first half, and then "But when alone with their evil associates they say", and their words in that second place are given in full, "We are definitely with you" and "we were only mocking". The sources take the two halves one after another and ask what is being described, since one tongue is behind both, and the answer is that the second half is the one that tells what the first was. The word used for the associates covers every thing a person keeps to themselves when no one is watching, and one line of commentary puts it as devils, and another as the great among them who had no part in this faith at all. The occasion is then set out at length in one of the sources, a going out with the believers and a joke told on the way back, which is why the verse is read as a warning about a policy rather than about a belief, since the policy needs two company and cannot keep both. One gloss stops on the grammar of the first words and explains what has been dropped from the verb, and the spiritual reading asks what a person is holding who can stand in both places at once, and answers that they wanted a relation with each side and were left with neither. Then the mockery is met by something other than mockery in the verse after this.
