([As Shaytan (Satan) has barred them from Allah's way] so they do not prostrate before Allah, Who brings to light what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you reveal. Allah, La ilaha illa Huwa (none has the right to be worshipped but He), the Lord of the Supreme Throne!)(27:25-26).

**What else the same passage holds.**

And He taught Adam all the names (of everything), then He showed them to the angels and said, "Tell Me the names of these if you are truthful. "Glory is to You, we have no knowledge except what you have taught us. Inform them of their names," and when he had informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the Ghayb (unseen) in the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing? One should note a subtle suggestion here in the use of two words. In asking the angels for the names of things, Allah said, "Tell Me"; but in commanding Adam to do so, He said, : It is thus an indication of his superiority over them. Another thing the episode indicates is that an increase or decrease is possible in the degree of knowledge the angels possess, for they were given, through Adam at least a primary knowledge about a thing which they did not know before.

34.text:
The command, the obedience and the refusal are in one sentence here, and the weight of the verse falls on the clause that separates them. "And remember when We said to the angels" is again a reminder rather than a first telling, and the address includes them as a body. "Prostrate before Adam" states the act and its direction in three words, and the sources dwell on that direction, since the prostration is to Adam and not of worship to him, a distinction the legal discussions need. "so they all did" is given without exception among the angels and without any description of reluctance, and the commentators notice that the text keeps the angels alone here, though other beings stand in the same account. "but not Iblîs" is the hinge, and the verse does not name a reason yet. "who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful" then gives the three steps in one clause, the refusal, the arrogance, and the unfaithfulness it ends in. The order is stopped at, since the refusal comes first and the pride after it, and the sources take the last word of the clause as the outcome rather than the motive, so the verse does not have to say what he believed. What he was asked to do is treated as an honour laid on Adam and a test of the hearers at the same time, and the excuses given in the verses that follow, a difference of material and a claim of precedence, are what the legal and spiritual discussions work with here, one of them ruling on the direction of a prostration and the other on what pride does to a person who knows the command.

**The command to prostrate.**

And mention when We said to the angels ‘Prostrate yourselves to Adam’ a prostration that is a bow of salutation; so they prostrated themselves except Iblīs the father of the jinn who was among the angels he refused to prostrate and disdained became proud and said I am better than he Q. 712; and so he became one of the disbelievers according to God’s knowledge. (And when We said unto the angels: Prostrate yourselves before Adam), a prostration of salutation, (they fell prostrate, all save Iblis. He demurred through pride) to follow his Lord's command. Allah reveals that He told the angels to prostrate to Adam out of recognition and respect, so they prostrated to him, eager to do as He told them, except for Iblīs, or Satan, who was originally from the jinn.

**To Adam, and in what sense.**

With regard to the question of prostration, we may add that, according to some authentic scholars, Salah, the basic form of Islamic worship, comprises of four kinds of actions - standing upright, bowing, sitting down, and prostrating oneself; the first two of these, standing up and sitting down, are actions which one habitually does in the course of one's daily chores, and which one also performs as acts of worship in the course of a Salah (prayer), but the other two, bowing down and prostrating oneself, are actions which one does not go through as a matter of habit, and which are characteristically associated with Salah (prayer) and Ibadah (worship); hence it is that the Islamic Shari'ah has identified them with acts of worship, and forbidden the Muslims to bow down or prostrate themselves before anyone other than Allah. But the Holy Qur'an mentions the angels alone, because when superior beings like the angels were required to show their respect for Adam inferior creatures like the jinns must, it goes without saying, have been ordered to do the same.

**Was Iblîs one of the angels.**

Although Iblis was not an angel, he was trying - and pretending - to imitate the angels' behavior and deeds, and this is why he was also included in the command to the angels to prostrate before Adam. It is also said that it was in Allah's foreknowledge that Satan was to become a disbeliever; as it is said that he was the first unbeliever ever. Due to the excellence of his worship, Allah had entered Iblīs into the company of the angels; but he then returned to his lowly nature, refusing to prostrate as Allah told him to, and becoming proud towards Adam, leading to him becoming a disbeliever. The command came to the angels, "All of you go to Adam's throne and prostrate yourself before Adam.

**Refused, acted arrogantly, became unfaithful.**

(And so became a disbeliever) after this because he refused to comply with Allah's command. He said, 'I was created from fire, and he was created from clay.' Therefore, the first error ever committed was arrogance, for the enemy of Allah was too arrogant to prostrate before Adam. The word literally means one who was far from the truth, and from the mercy of God.

**Two rulings that hang off this verse.**

For example, making pictures of living things has been totally banned; prostrating oneself before somebody, even as a mark of respect, has been forbidden; it is not permissible to offer one's Salah (prayer) at those hours of the day which the infidels had reserved for worshipping their gods, for even this slight and external correspondence might lead to 'association'; and, according to a Hadith reported by Muslim, one is not allowed to call one's slave an " abd" nor is a slave allowed to call his master a "rabb " - the words respectively signify "a slave" and 'one who gives nurture', and are as such harmless, but they can be misconstrued, and may mislead ignorant slaves or helpless and subjugated people into the worship of their masters: hence the prohibition. The word literally means one who was far from the truth, and from the mercy of God.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The episode recounted in the foregoing verses has shown how the angels came to learn that Adam was superior to them in so far as he possessed the forms of knowledge necessary for the function of divine vice regency, while they themselves did not, nor did the jinns. Now, Allah willed to manifest this superiority in a visible and concrete form. So, He commanded the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam in his honour. They obeyed except Iblis or Satan who, in his pride, refused to do so. If we go by the words of the Holy Qur'an, the command was given to the angels alone, but, in excepting Iblis from those who obeyed, the text also suggests that the command was given to all the created beings that existed at that time and possessed understanding, including the jinns as well as the angels. In this verse, the angels have been commanded to prostrate themselves before Adam . Another verse of the Holy Qur'an tells us that the parents and the brothers of Yusuf (Joseph) on reaching Egypt, prostrated themselves before him (12:100). Evidently such a prostration cannot have been intended as an act of worship, for worshipping anyone other than Allah is an act of association (Shirk) and infidelity (Kufr), and hence cannot possibly be allowed by any Shari ah. So, it appears that in the days of the ancient prophets prostrating oneself before somebody must have been just an act of courtesy or a way of showing one's respect, and enjoyed the same value as we do in our own days things like a simple greeting, a handshake, the kissing of hand, or standing up in someone's honour.

35.text:
Everything in this verse is permission except one clause, and the order matters because the exception is what the next verses turn on. "We cautioned, O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please" opens with warning rather than with the gift, and the two halves are quoted together here because the permission is the shape the warning sits inside, and the sources note the word for caution here, since what follows sounds like a favour. "Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please" gives the dwelling as shared, the wife named in the same breath, and the eating without reckoning; the commentators take "as freely as you please" to cover whatever they wanted, in any part of the Garden, and the permission to eat is treated as the general rule from which the prohibition is an exception. "but do not approach this tree" is then not a second command but the edge of the first, and the wording, approach rather than eat, is stopped at more than once. "or else you will be wrongdoers" ends without naming a punishment at all, which is how the discussion of what the prohibition actually lays on them begins, since the consequence is stated as a condition of the act and not as a sentence. The dwelling with his wife is taken by the sources as the first of the permissions in this passage and the pair are named together on purpose, and the verse after this records the slip.

**Dwell, and eat freely.**

And We said ‘Adam dwell anta ‘you’ of ‘dwell you’ here reiterates the concealed pronoun of the person of the verb uskun so that it wa-zawjuk may be made a supplement to it; and your wife Eve Hawwā’ — who was created from his left rib — in the Garden and eat thereof of its food easefully of anything without restrictions where you desire; but do not come near this tree to eat from it and this was wheat or a vine or something else lest you be become evildoers’ that is transgressors. Allah told Adam to live with his wife, Eve, in the Garden, with nothing to ruin their bliss.

**The scope of the permission.**

In allowing Adam and Hawwa to eat at pleasure, and in forbidding them to go near the tree, Allah used, according to the text of the Holy Qur'an, the verbs for the dual number, thus including both in the address. But the words of the Holy Qur'an do not exclude the other interpretation that both the events took place in Paradise, but that he had not been told at that time where he was to live, which was done later.

**What the words do not exclude.**

When Adam and Hawwa were sent to live in Paradise, they were allowed to eat whatever they liked 'at pleasure' - the Arabic word in the text being 'Raghadan' ‌ which signifies provision for which one does not have to work, and which is never exhausted nor falls short. (And We said: O Adam! Dwell thou and thy wife in the Garden) enter you and Eve into Paradise (and eat ye freely (of the fruits) without restriction (thereof where ye will) and whenever you will; (but come not near this tree) but do not eat from this tree, the tree of knowledge, which includes all types and kinds (lest ye become of the wrong-doers), lest you harm yourselves.

**Approach, not eat.**

They were instructed to consume the delightful food from anywhere in the Garden, but also to avoid going near a particular tree which they were forbidden to eat from. If they ate from the prohibited tree, they would become wrongdoers for disobeying Him.

**The end of the warning, and the test that follows.**

(Then the Shaytan made them slip therefrom) either refers to Paradise, and in this case, it means that Shaytan led Adam and Hawwa' away from it, as 'Asim bin Abi An-Najud recited it. Then Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the story of Adam and Eve, saying: Either they would follow the example of the angels and bow to God’s commandments, even if it meant bowing before someone they held inferior to themselves; or else they would be proud like Satan, and refuse to bow to others. This is the test that man faces throughout his entire life. When Adam woke up and saw Hawwa' next to him, it was claimed, he said, 'My flesh and blood, my wife.' Hence, Adam reclined with Hawwa'.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This is a continuation of the story of Adam . When his superiority over the angels and his fitness for the role of vice regent had been announced to the angels and been acknowledged by them, and Iblis had been condemned as an infidel and expelled from Paradise on account of his pride and his defiance of divine authority, Adam and Hawwa , his wife, received a command from Allah to live in Paradise and enjoy its blessings. But they were also instructed not to eat the fruit of a particular tree. Now, having been disgraced because of Adam Iblis or Satan had an account to settle with him, and as soon as he got the opportunity, he tricked them into eating from this tree. Because of this error on their part, they too were ordered to leave Paradise, and to go down and live on the earth. They were at the same time warned that their existence on the earth would no longer be full of perpetual bliss as it had been in Paradise, but that there would be dissension and enmity among men, their progeny, which would spoil the joy of earthly life. Since these events took place after Adam had been created and the angels had been commanded to prostrate themselves before him, some scholars have concluded from it that the creation of Adam and the prostration of the angels took place somewhere outside Paradise, and that he was sent there later on. Thus, their life was totally free from all care. They were commanded not to go near a certain tree - which was an emphatic way of asking them not to eat its fruit. The tree has not been given a specific name either in the Holy Qur'an or in the Hadith. Some commentators say that it was wheat, others say that it was a fig-tree or a grape-vine. But it is not really necessary to make specific what the Holy Qur'an has left vague. As to the apple being the fruit concerned, it is only a popular misunderstanding arising from the fact that the Latin word "Malum" means an "apple" as well as a "sin, or evil. According to the Holy Qur'an, it was Satan who 'caused them to slip' (azallahuma). It clearly shows that the error and disobedience of Adam and Hawwa was not of the kind which technically constitutes a sin, but arose out of a misunderstanding produced by Satan. They ate the forbidden fruit, because Satan had cleverly deceived them.16 We may note that in the previous episode the Holy Qur'an used the name Iblis a word which comes from the root Balas 'to be disappointed', and hence signifies "one who has lost all hope of receiving the grace of Allah.

36.text:
The verse begins with the deception itself: "But Satan deceived them". Deception is the right word, because nothing in the sentence states that Satan forced anyone or overpowered them. He worked on them with a suggestion, and the suggestion was enough to move them from where they stood. "leading to their fall from the blissful state they were in" then names what the deception produced, and it is stated as a fall, a drop out of a condition of ease, before anything is said about the sentence itself. The verse does not describe the sentence first. It describes the loss, and only then the command. "and We said" is the turn, the point where the speech moves from what Satan did to what the Lord ordered, and the order is given plainly. "Descend from the heavens to the earth as enemies to each other" tells them where they go and in what relation to one another, and the words "as enemies to each other" are the part the rest of the chapter keeps returning to: the human and the Satan will be opposed in the world below. "You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay" closes the sentence with what they will have there: "You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay", a home, a provision and a term that is fixed. So the sending down is a settled place for a set time, not a casting out without end. The verse before gave the garden and its ease, and the verse after turns to the words that Adam is given, so this verse is the hinge between the garden and the earth.

**What the slip was.**

(But the Devil caused them to deflect), caused them to slip (therefrom), from Paradise, (and expelled them from the state in which they were), from the comfort which they had enjoyed; (and We said) to Adam, Eve, the peacock and the serpent (Fall down) go down to the earth, (one of you a foe unto the other! There shall be for you on earth a habitation), a dwelling-place, (and a provision), a benefit and livelihood, (for a time) until the moment of death. Then Satan Iblīs caused them to slip he caused them to be removed fa-azallahumā a variant reading has fa-azālahumā he caused them to be away from it therefrom that is from the Garden when he said to them ‘Shall I point you to the tree of eternity’ cf. When God made Adam stand up in front of the angels including Iblis (Satan), and tested them by commanding them to bow down before Adam, He was giving the first man on earth a practical demonstration of the two paths that would be open to his progeny.

**The oath Satan swore.**

Q. 20120 and swore to them by God that he was only giving good advice to them and so they ate of it; and brought them out of what they were in of bliss; and We said ‘Go down to earth both of you and all those comprised by your seed; some of you of your progeny an enemy to the other through your wronging one another; and in the earth a dwelling a place of settlement shall be yours and enjoyment of whatever of its vegetation you may enjoy for a while’ until the time your terms of life are concluded. According to the Holy Qur'an, Satan assured them on oath that he was one of their well-wishers (7:21). Satan did not stop whispering to them, trying to trick them, until he made them slip and fall by eating from the tree which Allah had told them not to.

**Who was sent down, and where.**

Dwell you and your wife in the Paradise and eat both of you freely with pleasure and delight, of things therein wherever you will, but come not near this tree or you both will be of the Zalimin (wrongdoers). In actual fact, they were 'brought out' under a divine command, but since Satan served as a means and as an intermediary, the action has been attributed to him.17. (Allah created Adam tall, with thick hair, just as a date tree with full branches. When Adam ate from the forbidden tree, his cover fell off, and the first thing that appeared was his private area. When he saw his private area, he ran away in Paradise and his hair got caught in a tree. He tried to free himself and Ar-Rahman called him, 'O Adam! Are you running away from Me?' When Adam heard the words of Ar-Rahman (Allah), he said, 'No, O my Lord! But I am shy.')

**Whether Satan had already been in Paradise.**

But if Satan, as some scholars maintain, had already been expelled, then the addressees are Adam and Hawwa' and their progeny; the implication would now be that Adam and Hawwa ' would have to undergo a double punishment, firstly that of being banished from Paradise, secondly that of seeing enmity arise among their children which must make life unpleasant for parents. The majority of scholars said that Shaytan was originally prohibited from entering Paradise, but there were times when he sneaked into it in secret.

**Two alternative courses set before them.**

Either they would follow the example of the angels and bow to God’s commandments, even if it meant bowing before someone they held inferior to themselves; or else they would be proud like Satan, and refuse to bow to others. Here on earth man is constantly faced with two alternative courses of action. He can either follow the course set by the angels and carry out God’s commandments by bowing before truth and justice in all that he does; or he can act as Satan did and, letting himself be controlled by arrogance and contempt, refuse to concede the right of others.

**What else the same passage holds.**

A question arises here as to how Satan got into Paradise for seducing Adam and Hawwa when he had already been expelled from there for refusing to prostrate himself. There are many possible ways in which he can have played his trick. Possibly he never met them, but planted the suggestion in their minds from afar - a thing which Satan can always do, and of which we have a specimen in the work of the hypnotists. It is equally possible that Satan, being one of the jinns whom Allah has given certain unusual powers denied to man, assumed the shape of a snake or of something else, and thus succeeded in entering Paradise. Perhaps it was because of this disguise that Adam did not remember Allah's warning that Satan was his enemy. It apparently suggests that he did actually meet them, and speak to them face o face.

37.text:
Then Adam was inspired with words of prayer by his Lord, and the words came to him from outside himself, as a gift from his Lord and not as something he worked out. "so He accepted his repentance" is the result, and the word "so" matters: the acceptance follows from the words, and the words are the way the return was made. "Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" then gives the reason in a description of God, not of Adam. The verse turns the whole matter onto the Lord. He is the one who accepts, and He is the one who is merciful, and the two titles in the last phrase are the ground of what was done. The verse before ended with the earth and the stay, and here the stay has begun. The verse does not say in the same breath what the words were, and the sources differ about that, which is where the headings below pick up. What the verse does say is that the first man was not left under the fall, because the way back was given to him as well as the fall. So this sentence is one of return, placed straight after the sentence of descent, so that the reader sees both at once.

**What the words were.**

In the last three verses and of these four, Allah reminds the Israelites of the blessings He has bestowed upon them, and invites them to Islam and to good deeds. "O Children of Israel" repeats the address of the earlier verse, and the repetition is a way of holding the same people to the same memory. The people are reminded of the gift in its own terms, before any demand is made of them, because a demand made to people who have forgotten the gift would be heard as a burden and not as the return of a debt, so the reader sees the favour first and the test of it afterwards. The memory asked for here is the first step in the covenant. Without it, the demands that follow have no ground, and the verse makes that link plain by putting the call to remember at its head.

"And remember when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes" is the third and most vivid of the favours, and the sentence is built as a sequence of three acts. The first is the parting of the sea, which opens a way where none existed. The second is the rescue, which is the favour done to the people who are walking through. The third is the drowning, which is the same event seen from the other side, and the verse puts it in the same sentence so that the reader does not forget who was saved and who was lost. "before your very eyes" is the closing phrase, and it is the one that makes the witness personal. The verse does not claim that the event was carried to them by others. It names that they saw it, so the favour is theirs by sight and not by hearsay. The verse before named the rescue from the people of Pharaoh, and this verse names the place where that rescue happened, which is the sea. The verse after moves from the favours to the story of the calf, so this verse is the last of the three acts of deliverance before the account turns to the failure that followed them.

51.text:
"And remember when We appointed forty nights for Moses" opens with the memory again, and this time the memory is of an appointment, a fixed period set apart by the Lord for a particular purpose. The verse does not say that Moses went up to receive the Scripture on a whim. It names that the nights were appointed, which means they had a limit and an end, and a people who waited for them were waiting for a term that had been set. "then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully" is the turn, and it is joined to the appointment by the word "then", so the failure follows the time of waiting directly. The phrase "in his absence" is the key to the whole sentence. The people did not turn away while Moses was in their midst. They turned while he was out of sight, and the verse makes the absence the occasion of the fault. The closing words describe the judgement on what they did, and the verse does not soften it or explain it away. It names the act and the wrong in the same breath, so the wrong is not a slip of the mind but a deed done with the Scripture still on its way. The verse before ended with the favour of the sea, and this verse sets a second favour beside it, the appointment and the Scripture, so the reader sees the gift and the failure side by side.

52.text:

53.text:
And remember when We gave Moses the Scripture carries the memory forward from the calf to the book. The verse does not say the Scripture came as a reward for anything. It says that it came, and the word "remember" asks the reader to hold the gift beside the wrong just named, so that the two sit in the same frame. The Scripture here is the Torah given to Moses, and the sources take it to be the book of the law that the Children of Israel were to live by. The clause that follows, "the standard to distinguish between right and wrong that perhaps you would be rightly guided", carries the word the verse uses for the criterion and tells you what the book is for. The standard is a measure by which one thing can be told from another. The people who had just worshipped the calf had lost the ability to tell the true from the false, and the book is given as the means of getting it back. The clause closes the sentence with the purpose, and the word "perhaps" in it is not a doubt about the Lord's intention. It is the form of an aim, a wish on the Lord's side that the people choose the guidance the book offers, and the choice is left to them. So the sentence moves from memory, to gift, to the nature of the gift, to its purpose, and each phrase is a step on the same road. The verse before, 2:52, ended with a pardon given so that the people would be thankful. This verse carries that thanks forward into the means of guidance, so the reader sees the Scripture as the form the gratitude is to take. The sentence is also a point of return in the account. The people have been shown the calf and the pardon, and now they are shown what they were given in place of the image they had made, a book to judge by rather than a figure to bow to.

**What the Scripture was.**

The sources agree on the identity of the book. One short commentary reads the Scripture as the Torah, and the Torah is named again in the commentary on the same verse, which places the gift of the book after the forty nights and the forgiveness, so that the order of events is the order of the verses. The commentary on the Torah given to Sayyidna Mūsā makes the same identification and adds that the Torah is a book of Allah and not a human writing. That is the first thing the verse establishes. The book is not the product of the people's reflection, and it is not a set of customs that grew up among them. It is given from outside, to a prophet, and it is given to a people who had just shown how badly they judge when left to themselves. The gift of the book is therefore a correction to the calf and to the forty nights, and the sources read the sequence as deliberate.

**Furqān, the criterion.**

The word the translation renders as the standard is furqān, and the commentary on it is the longest in the block. The commentary on the Torah gives three readings that the sources allow. It may mean the rulings of the law found in the Torah, since the law settles the differences that arise over belief and over right action. It may mean the signs and miracles that decide between a true claim and a false one in a way that can be seen. Or it may mean the Torah itself, which is at once the book of Allah and the instrument by which truth is separated from falsehood. The commentary on the Torah, in the sense it gives the word, takes it as what differentiates between truth and falsehood, guidance and deviation. The lawful-and-unlawful commentary narrows the sense to the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and the prohibitions, and adds other things that the book carries. These are not three separate books. They are three ways of naming one function, which is to make a difference that can be acted on. The verse uses the word once, and the commentaries keep returning to it because a criterion is useful only if it can be applied in practice.

**The guidance it was for.**

The verse ends with the hope of guidance, and the sources take that hope as the true purpose of the book. The short commentary treats the giving as one of the blessings of Allah, and places the purpose in the guidance a person draws from the book to the truth. the commentary on the forty days, in the same vein, reads the phrase so that you may be guided aright as set after escaping the sea, which links the book to the deliverance that came before it and to the land that follows. The Qurʾān in the other chapter of al-Aʿrāf says the Scripture was an enlightenment, a guidance and a mercy, and the sources bring that into this verse as a reminder that guidance is the purpose and mercy is its form. The commentary on piety gives the content of the guidance in plain terms: to worship God alone, to believe in Him without having seen Him, to fear the Day of Judgement, to take only the pure things of the earth, and to keep oneself from sin. It is those who take up this way of life, the source says, who will prosper in the next world. The commentary does not separate the guidance of the book from the way of life that the book requires.

**Remember the order of favours.**

The verse is the third of a short run that begins with the forty nights, and the run is one account read in sequence. the commentary on the forty days quotes Allah's own speech, remember My favour upon you when I forgave you for worshipping the calf, and places the appointment of Moses at the end of the forty days that were added to the thirty nights mentioned in another chapter. He also gives the month as Dhū al-Qaʿdah with the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. The sources do not claim more about the calendar than the verses themselves give, and the point the commentary keeps is the order: the people were delivered, they worshipped the calf in the absence, they were pardoned, and then the book was given. Read in that order, the book is the answer to the calf rather than a separate matter, and the reader is asked to see the sequence before taking the lesson from it.

**Discernment in the heart.**

The allusive reading of the verse, moves the criterion from the book to the inward faculty that the book is meant to form. The commentator says that the discernment was given to Moses's people outwardly, and that the same discernment was placed in the inwardness of the community of the Prophet. He describes the discernment as something that appears in a person's inner life, and that purifies the aspiration of the one who has it. These sayings are not a ruling and they settle nothing about the law. They are a reading of what the criterion does to the reader who receives it, and the commentary is careful to present them as allusion rather than as a claim about what the book says. Read beside the legal sense, the allusion adds one thing: a book that separates truth from falsehood outside a person has to be matched by a faculty inside him that can use it, and the verse asks for both.

54.text:
The verse opens on the speaker and the people he is speaking to: "And remember when Moses said to his people". The calf is what gives him the need to address them at all, and this is not a voice from outside the community but the prophet speaking to his own folk, the ones who made the image and bowed before it. "O my people!" comes first, and the phrase carries affection inside the rebuke that follows. "Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf" is the charge, and the verb is turned back on the people, so the wrong is not done to Moses or to the Lord but to themselves. The charge names the act, worship of the calf, and places the injury in the soul of the one who worshipped. "so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute the calf-worshippers among yourselves" is the remedy, and it is a hard one. The turn to repentance is the way back, and the words about execution are the cost the people are asked to carry as part of returning. The verse does not pretend the way back is easy. "That is best for you in the sight of your Creator" gives the reason the hard remedy is the better course: it is best in the sight of the One who made them, which is the measure that counts. "Then He accepted your repentance" turns the sentence from command to result. The people did what was asked, and the Lord accepted it. "Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" closes the verse on the Lord's nature, the one who receives the return and is merciful in receiving it. The verse before gave the book as the standard, and this verse shows the people using that standard in the hard hour: they are asked to judge their own offence by it and to return.

(and kill (the guilty) among yourselves) let those who did not worship the calf kill those who worshipped it. This was the repentance required from the Children of Israel for worshipping the calf. Then the Israelites acted upon this divine commandments, they became worthy of receiving the mercy and favour of Allah in the other world. 55.text:
"And remember when you said, O Moses!" turns the address to the people again, this time in their own voice, and what they put into words is a demand. The speech is addressed to Moses by name, so the demand is made to the one who has just brought them the Scripture, in his own presence. "We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes" is the whole claim, set down in the first person, so the reader hears them making it. The demand is not for a sign that might confirm the message. It asks to see the Lord directly and openly, and the sentence joins belief to that sight, so that belief is made conditional on something they have set. "so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on" is the answer, and the verse makes the answer a thing that happened in plain view. The phrase "while you were looking on" is the key, because it is the watching that is punished, not the speaking alone. They were looking when it struck, and the verse does not let the reader forget that the people were present at their own judgement. The verse before ended with the return accepted, and this verse goes back to an earlier stage of the same people, when they were still refusing the one who brought them the message. Read in order, the two verses show the same community at two moments, a refusal and then a return, and the sources keep both in view.

**Seeing Allah with their eyes.**

(And (remember) when you said: "O Musa ! We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly.") means, "Publicly", "So that we gaze at Allah. Demanding to see the Essence without divine blessing is an open act of sacrilege which is one of the signs of distance and misery whereas attest ing to the attribute of [divine] governance in the unveilings of might as linked to the kindnesses of nearness is one of the marks of communion and the tokens of felicity.

**The thunderbolt and the watching.**

(While you were looking) means, "Some of them were struck with lightning while others were watching. Al-Qurtubi said that this is what is correct, because, he said, although the Children of Israel witnessed these tremendous calamities and incidents, that did not mean that they were not responsible for fulfilling the commandments any more. Also, remember when you shamelessly addressed Moses ﷺ, saying that you would not believe him until you saw Allah with your own eyes, in the open before you, and the lightning struck you and killed you, whilst some of you looked at the others.

Then Sayyidna Musa (Moses) brought the Torah from Mount Tur (Sinai) and presented it to the Israelites as the book of Allah, some of them were insolent enough to say that they could not believe it until and unless Allah Himself told them in so many words. Arriving there, they heard the words of Allah with their own ears. (Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful), and said, "Musa said to them, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' He said, 'What is the matter with you' They said, 'The problem is that we died and came back to life.' He said, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' So Allah sent some angels who made the mountain topple over them."

**The demand made in ignorance.**

Surely when they spoke from ignorance without any sense whatsoever of shame the convulsion and the thunderbolt blast overtook them. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin. "Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful" is the reversal of the thunderbolt, and it is stated in one sentence with its purpose attached. "Then" joins the restoring to the striking before it, so the life given back follows the death directly. The word "after your death" names the state from which they were brought, and the verse does not hide that it was a real death and not a faint. It states that the life was given so that they might be thankful, which keeps the favour in the register of thanks and not of reward. The sentence is short and it carries the whole of the return, from the death of the watching to the life of the gratitude, so the reader is asked to measure the one against the other.

57.text:
"And remember when We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, saying" begins with the call to memory again, and then the favour is laid out in three acts. The first is the shade, cloud over people in an open land, which is a protection given before anything is asked of them. The second is the food, manna and quails sent down, which is the provision that keeps the people alive in the wilderness. The third is the instruction that comes with it: "Eat from the good things We have provided for you". The command is to eat, and the goodness of the food is named as the thing the Lord has provided. "The evildoers certainly did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves" then turns to the response, and the sentence makes the same move as the verse about the calf. The people did not harm the Lord by their ingratitude, since nothing given to them could be taken from Him by their refusal. They harmed themselves, and the verse states so in the same breath as the favour. The contrast is built into the sentence, so the reader sees the gift and the failure to take it as one movement. The verse before gave life after death, and this verse gives the food and the shade that keep that life going. The shade comes first in the sentence and the food second, and the order is the order of need: a people in the open needs shelter from the sun before it needs bread, and the Lord supplies both. The two together show the favour continuing after the return.

**The clouds for shade.**

Another of Allah’s blessings was that He sent clouds to shade you from the heat of the sun when you were wandering the earth; and He sent down manna, a sweet drink similar to honey, and quails for you, telling you to consume of the good things He had provided you with. And We made the cloud overshadow you that is We sheltered you with fine clouds from the heat of the sun while you were in the wilderness; and We sent down in them the clouds upon you manna and quails — which are respectively a type of citrus known as turunjabīn and the quail — and We said ‘Eat of the good things We have provided for you’ and do not store any of it away but they were not grateful for this favour and stored the food and so they were deprived of it; And they did not wrong Us in this but themselves they wronged since the evil consequences of this befell them. (And We caused the white cloud to overshadow you) in the wilderness (and sent down on you honey and quails) also in the wilderness, (Eat of the good things) of the lawful things (wherewith We have provided you) that We have given you and do not keep any provision for future days.

**Manna and quails in the wilderness.**

That is why the wilderness is called Tih which signifies 'having lost one's way'. When they began to starve, Allah blessed them with Mann (manna) and Salwa . Then, quails would not flee but come around them, so that they could catch the birds with little effort.

**Eat of the good things.**

(Eat of the good lawful things We have provided for you,)(7:160) this form of command is a simple order of allowance, guiding to what is good. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin.

**Wronged themselves, not Us.**

(And they did not wrong Us but they wronged themselves) means, 'We commanded them to eat from what We gave them, and to perform the acts of worship (but they rebelled).' This Ayah is similar to Allah's statement,. Their ingratitude and disbelief for these blessings did not affect Allah in any way, but they wronged themselves, losing their share from the good they had done and exposing themselves to suffering.

**Food saved against the days.**

Yet they did save food for future days-(They wronged us not) by saving food, (but they did wrong themselves) they harmed themselves. The Israelites started on the expedition, but, on approaching Syria, when they came to learn about the military strength of the foe, their courage failed them, and they refused to engage themselves in the Jihad. "Look at what I did with the Children of Israel, how many blessings I poured down upon them, how much I caressed them in that empty desert!

**What else the same passage holds.**

These two incidents took place in the wilderness of Tih. And We shaded you with clouds and sent down on you Al-Manna and the quail, (saying): The Israelites belonged to Syria, but had gone to Egypt in the time of Sayyidna Yusuf (Joseph), and settled there, while Syria itself had come under the domination of a people called the Amaliqah (Amaleks). "Eat of the good lawful things We have provided for you," (but they rebelled). When the Pharaoh had been drowned and the Israelites could live in peace, Allah commanded them to go to war against the Amaliqah, and to free their homeland. And they did not wrong Us but they wronged themselves Allah punished them for their disobedience, so that for full forty years they kept wandering about in a wilderness, and could not even go back to Egypt. The wilderness was not very vast, but only a stretch of some ten miles, lying between Egypt and Syria. They would make a day-long march in the direction of Egypt, and stop somewhere for the night. But, on getting up the next morning, they would always find themselves just where they had started from. Thus, they spent forty years wandering about in the wilderness in futile rage and exasperation. The wilderness was just a barren space without a tree or a building which could offer protection against heat or cold. There was no food to eat, and no clothes to wear. But in answer to the prayer of Sayyidna Musa Allah made a miraculous provision for all their needs. When they could not bear the scorching sun, Allah sent them the shade of a thin, white cloud. That is to say, Allah produced honeydew in abundance which they could easily gather. Hence it has been designated as mann which signifies "a gift or favour". The two things being unusual, the Holy Qur'an says that Allah made them "descend" for the benefit of the Israelites. Similarly, when they were thirsty, Allah commanded Sayyidna Musa to strike a rock with his staff, which made twelve streams gush forth, as the Holy Qur'an narrates in another place. When they complained of the thick darkness of the night, Allah produced for them a constant pillar of light. When their clothes began to wear out, Allah showed another miracle - their clothes would neither go dirty nor wear out, while the clothes of the children grew with their growth. Allah had commanded the Israelites to take as much of the miraculous food as they really needed, and not to store it for future use. After Allah mentioned the calamities that He saved the Children of Israel from, He mentioned the favors that He granted them, saying, But when they disobeyed this commandment, the meat began to rot. This is how they harmed, not Allah, but themselves. This Ayah mentions the white clouds that provided shade for the Children of Israel, protecting them from the sun's heat during their years of wandering. In the Hadith about the trials, An-Nasai recorded Ibn Abbas saying, Allah shaded the Children of Israel with clouds during the years of wandering.
